utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Case Number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, counsel in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Mathias Neuner, Daryl Mundis, assisted by Andres Vatter, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the appearances for Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic and Alex Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have the appearances for the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, Nermin Mulalic, and Rodney Dixon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to greet everyone on behalf of the Chamber, the Prosecution, Defence counsel. I see that one of the Defence is missing. Nevertheless, I greet everyone else in the courtroom and outside the courtroom. We'll be hearing another witness for the Defence today, but the Chamber would like to provide you with some information before we start hearing the witness. Could we first go into private session, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now that we're in open session the Trial Chamber has three decisions to render. Firstly, with regard to the issue that concerns the Defence's request to respond to the Prosecution's submissions on facts admitted in other cases, adjudicated facts. Having deliberated, we give the Defence one week to prepare its submissions. So you have until next Wednesday to respond. And we will render our written decision at a subsequent date. Our second decision -- it's a pity that we haven't numbered our oral decisions because we have already rendered a significant number of decisions. But nevertheless, this decision which doesn't have a number is as follows. I'll read it out very slowly so that everyone can follow. It concerns whether or not a document of the 25th -- 24th and 25th of May can be admitted. It's addressed the 3rd Corps and it's signed by the duty officer. The Trial Chamber admits this document into evidence only for the refreshment of witness's memory, but the Chamber would also like to point out that this document shall be admitted only because it was used to refresh a witness's memory. And it will be used subsequently by the Judges only to allow the Judges to be aware of the previous debate on the refreshment of the witness's memory. Mr. Registrar, could we have an exhibit number that naturally subject to the reservations I have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. P951 will be the exhibit number and the English version P951/E. It will be admitted with the conditions that you have just set forth. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. There is also another decision that I would like to render which concerns the documents that the translation unit was required to provide. A memo was sent to CLSS and CLSS has done the work they were asked to do. This concerns P662/E. So there is a memo that concerns this document. And, Mr. Registrar, we need a number for the Chamber that was a memo from CLSS dated the 7th of February, and there is a second memo from CLSS dated the 14th of February, 2005, which concerns DH165.6 and P839/E. So, Mr. Registrar, could we have two exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The internal memo from CLSS dated the 7th of February, 2005, which concerns Prosecution Exhibit P662/E should be admitted into evidence as the Chamber's document. The number will be C8. As far as the second certainly memo is concerned dated the 14th of February, 2005, which concerns Defence document 165.6 and P839/E, a Prosecution document, this shall be admitted into evidence as number C9. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The document is P439/E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. While we accept that this is a formal memorandum from the translation unit which must become part of the record because it is as a result of a request Your Honours have made, we have with the greatest respect to the translation unit, some serious questions to be raised about this particular document, and in my submission this is an appropriate time now to ask for a further request to be made to the translation unit. The reason being, Your Honour, is in our view the translation unit has not answered the question that Your Honours put to it, which is why are there two different meanings given to the same word. The translation unit maintains that the two meanings for the same word are ones that should be read for this text, but they do not explain why there are two different meanings given. And, Your Honour, we would request that you direct the translation unit to answer that very important question because that was the reason why this whole issue arose in the first place. In addition to that, Your Honour, what the translation unit has gone on to say is that the first use of the word "odnosno" where the 7th Brigade is mentioned can only be read in one way. But then when it comes to the second use of the word "odnosno" with HVO units, in the last paragraph they say well, that could be read either way, so it could have an alternative reading; but not the first one. In my submission, with the greatest respect, we cannot understand why they can come to that conclusion. Why can both places where "odnosno" is used not be read this both ways? That was our request in the first place: Is there an alternative meaning? They have said yes, there is an alternative meaning for the second word, but not for the first use. In our view, this doesn't help Your Honours at all to resolve the problem. I know great efforts have been made by the translation unit to look into this matter, but in our view, the matter is still not resolved. We would request a further submission be made to the translation to resolve those two questions, which is why the difference and can the word not be read both ways in both contexts. This is a free-standing word. We have a copy of the Croatian-English Dictionary here, and in that dictionary, Your Honour, it very clearly indicates that it can be read as "and." The translation did refer to in their memorandum but only to the first few lines of the dictionary definition. They never went on to show how the word can be used as one to show more than one item, a collective item. For example, in the dictionary definition, and I have a copy here for Your Honours, they give examples of someone who is 14 and 17 years old; somebody who is to meet somebody at 8.00 or 10.00, or 8.00 and 10.00. They give examples of two relatives, her aunt and her first cousin, for example. These are all examples that are mentioned in the dictionary definition which are not included in the memorandum from CLSS. Just one final point, Your Honours, that the CLSS was also asked to look at the transcript. I remember very clearly that Your Honours pointed them at the direction of looking at the full transcript where this word was used by the witness and in relation to the document, but it doesn't appear from their memorandum that they have taken the transcript into account. And it might well be that that is an important consideration, to look at the context, the full context, of the word when giving it a definition. So for all of those reasons, despite all the work that has been done, we still don't believe this is of any assistance to us in re solving this problem and we would request that the matter has to be sent back to CLSS to resolve the matter for Your Honours. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Dixon. Is there anything the Prosecution would like to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution will take a slightly different stand on this issue, Mr. President, as you might anticipate. It's our position that CLSS within this institution has extremely high professional standards and given the length of time that these dedicated and hard-working individuals have put into interpreting and translating for us are among the best in the world. We don't believe that further work or analysis needs to be done with respect to this issue. They've been asked to do it twice; they have responded. They have explained in the memorandum C8 the position that they have taken. We believe to take this further or perhaps to outsource this document for further translation work, Mr. President, would not be a good idea. It could lead to what we in the common law often know of the battle of the experts, whereas the parties would be seeking outside expertise to explain to us what this document means when our own in-house linguistic experts have already done so. And finally, we would submit that many of the points made by my learned colleague, Mr. Dixon, are the types of issues in argument that come at the end of trial. Their position with respect to the language of the document is quite clear; the Prosecution position will be, as you can imagine, quite contrary to that put forward by the Defence. And in our submissions, CLSS has been asked to do this; they have done it. They have been asked to do it again; they have done that. We would submit that the position taken by the Defence is more properly left to the closing arguments once the Trial Chamber has all the evidence before it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Given the Defence's question, the Prosecution's position, the Judges will deliberate on the issue and we will inform you of our decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just add one further matter which may be of assistance. I do agree with my friend that these are matters of argument as well. We will be addressing those of course in the closing arguments, and that is in respect of what the witness himself said about it the document. Our submission would be that that is paramount: what he actually said about why he put these words and what he meant as the author of that document. Fortunately we had the author of that document to give evidence directly to Your Honours. As my friend as said before, the issue is whether we can obtain a neutral interpretation from the translation unit. And in our submission this document simply doesn't take us any closer to resolving that problem. And it's in everyone's interest, we would submit, that we have the questions we put to CLSS about what are the different meanings; can it be given different meanings in different contexts; why one meaning and not the other; all those questions that were put in the transcript. Those might be properly answered. And it might be a question of clarifying that with the translation unit. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, for the sake of the transcript and so that the Chamber is quite clear that General Hadzihasanovic's Defence doesn't have a neutral position with regard to this issue, we fully agree with the submissions made by my colleague, Mr. Dixon. We don't believe that the answer posed by the Chamber has been fully answered. We believe that we should condition to deal with the issue. This is in the interest of the Chamber and of everyone else. And finally, when you indicated that the translation unit should review the transcript, this was extremely important because the witness who drafted that document drafted other documents which -- in evidence and which show that these were two things that the 306th regarded in quite a different way -- in a separate way. So we don't understand how CLSS could have said that "odnosno" can be translated in one part of the text in different ways and in another part of the text they give it only one meaning. With all due respect, because I also believe that the translation unit is doing excellent work, but I must point out that before this Chamber we have on a number of occasions noticed significant errors which affect in a significant manner the meaning of documents. I believe that this is one such example and the Trial Chamber should endeavour to obtain a final answer to all the questions raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As I have said, the Judges will deliberate about the matter and we will inform you of our decision as soon as possible. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just -- if I could simply add one point and this is with respect to the transcript or sending -- having CLSS review the transcript of the witness's testimony. The Trial Chamber will recall at the time this was raised that the Prosecution did not believe that was a wise course of action for the simple reason that with respect to this document -- I draw your attention to the transcript at page 14860 where the witness himself said that he didn't draft the document but simply signed it. So our position would be that he's not the drafter. Whatever the testimony of the witness was with respect to what he thought he was signing is a matter for closing arguments. And in our opinion, since he is not the drafter, what he has to say about the document is of only limited value and we don't believe we should be getting into a situation where a large number of documents might be challenged or on the grounds that a drafter 10 or 12 years later tries to reinterpret a contemporaneously written document. We strongly believe that the documents need to speak for themselves. The witness's testimony concerning the documents is a matter for closing argument. And we would simply like to put that on the record as well, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is a part of the transcript personally -- I believe that this is as a result of fact that this is sui generis procedure. Mr. Dixon [sic] has said according to the common-law procedure that each party calls its own experts, whereas according to the continental system the Chamber would call an expert who would state his position as an expert independently. As this is a hybrid procedure, the solution that was found by those who drew up the Rules, the solution was to have a specialised service, CLSS namely. And it is their staff who do this work. But having pointed this out I -- I personally believe that when the parties call their witnesses or witness for the Defence or witness for the Prosecution, if they believe that a term in a document might result in significant debate and have subsequent consequences, nothing prevents the parties from calling an expert as a witness who will say that the word "odnosno" means such-and-such a thing. And then we would have a course on B/C/S grammar and on the term "odnosno." That could be the procedure to be followed. In spite of the existence of CLSS, we're not prevented from calling such a witness. The parties are not prevented from calling such a witness to support their point of view because if this debate is included in the submissions of the parties before the Chamber deliberates, then we won't have had an adversarial debate about the issues. So this is why it's important for both parties to intervene and this will make it possible for the Chamber to be familiar with the debate. But it's not useful for the Judges to discuss this matter among themselves [as interpreted]. But as I have already said, we will render our decision as soon as possible. If there are no other issues to raise, we will now call the witness. Mr. Usher, could you call the witness into the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Let me check first that you are hearing what I'm saying in your own language. If so, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you have been called as a Witness by the Defence of General Hadzihasanovic. Before you read the solemn declaration, I need to know your identity. So please tell me your first and last name, date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm Hilmo Ahmetovic. I was born on the 10th of February, 1964, in location Potocani, municipality of Doboj, today part of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is today your occupation and position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a graduate lawyer. I'm employed at the cantonal court in Zenica and working in that court.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Working in Zenica at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993, what was your position and role?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the beginning of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina I was working in a manufacturing company Bosanka Doboj as head of the legal department. And after the conflict broke out I moved to Tesanj where I became a member of the Territorial Defence which later developed into the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and I worked there until the 1st of September, 1992, when I became secretary of the district military prosecutor's office of Doboj based in Tesanj. And I performed those duties until February 1993 when I became a judge of the district military court of Doboj based in Tesanj. I kept that position until the 25th of October, 1993, when I became a judge of the district military court of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Have you testified before in an international or national court about the events that took place in your country in 1992 and 1993, or is this the first time for you to testify in court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time for me to appear as a witness in these cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask the usher to give you the solemn declaration and ask you kindly to read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, please take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, as I have said, you have been called by the Defence as a Defence witness. And before the give the floor to the Defence counsel which will have questions for you, I wish to give you some information regarding the proceedings with respect to witness testimony. As you will realise very quickly, this is a very specific procedure in which there's a combination of common law and continental law and the Rules of Procedure that guide us allows the Defence, which calls you, to ask you questions within the framework of what is known as the examination-in-chief. The Defence has envisaged a period of about an hour and a half for their questions. Yes, indeed, it is an hour and a half. The questions that will be put to you by Defence counsel are not leading; neutral in such a way that the witness is expected to give full answers to those questions. Upon the completion of that stage the Prosecution, which is to your right, will also have questions for you in the form of a cross-examination. This is a common law characteristic, and according to the common law they have an equal amount of time available to them. But an important difference is that the Prosecution is allowed during their cross-examination to ask you leading questions so that you may answer with a yes or no. So that is the technical aspect. At the end of that stage the Defence attorneys may have additional questions for you which are directly linked to the questions asked during the cross-examination. However, in that stage, too, the questions may not be leading. At the end of these stages, these three different stages, the Judges who are in front of you may ask you questions. And in view of the fact that you are a judge, I am sure that they will have plenty of questions for you. The Judges are allowed to ask you questions at any point in time, but they prefer to wait for both parties to finish with their questions because very often the concerns of the Judges are already covered by the parties. So we prefer to allow them to ask you questions first. And once that has been completed, if the Judges feel that there are points to be clarified because they feel that the answers are not quite clear enough, then they may ask you to clarify some of the answers you have given. All this is in the interest of justice and the establishment of the truth. And if certain questions which we feel should have been put to the witness were not and we consider them to be important in the interest of truth, we will ask you those questions. And also during the questions the parties may be showing you documents and you will be asked to comment on those documents. That would be, in very general terms, the way in which this hearing will develop. As you may know, we don't have any written document from you except for a very brief summary of your testimony. So what will represent your testimony will be what you said here which will be recorded in the transcript which will appear on the screen, as you will see. And that will be the record of this hearing. Hence, the importance of what you say. If you don't understand the meaning of a question put to you, ask the person putting it to rephrase it, but I'm sure that as a judge you will understand the sense of the questions. But as I say this to all witnesses, I'm saying this to you, too. I also need to remind witnesses of two important points in our rules, and that is that when a witness takes the solemn declaration to tell the whole truth, all false testimony is excluded; that is the first reminder. And the second which is specific to our procedure, and that is if a witness feels that if answering a question his answers may one day be used to incriminate him, the witness is entitled to say that he won't answer that question; but this is something we have never come across. So it is just a hypothetical. The Chamber may nevertheless ask the witness to provide an answer, guaranteeing immunity for the future. In the American system, immunity is granted by the Prosecution, but in our system it is the Trial Chamber. So those would be the general remarks regarding this hearing. We will also have two breaks of 20 to 25 minutes which are necessary because everything that is being said is being interpreted. So the interpreters need a rest, also to give the witness a chance to have a breather because answering questions for hours can be quite tiring. So you will have two breaks of 20, 25 minutes each. So those are the general points of information that I wanted to give you. I will now give the floor to the Defence counsel who will begin her examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Judge Ahmetovic.

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the information given to you by the Trial Chamber, let me ask you something else. We speak the same language and you can immediately answer my question, but I would appeal to you to wait a few seconds before answering my question so that both my question and your answer can be interpreted to Their Honours and our learned friends from the Prosecution can follow what we're saying. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, I will be using some of the documents in the binder from yesterday for this witness. I would like to ask this binder of documents to be given to the witness so as to avoid any future interruptions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Judge Ahmetovic, you said that for a time in 1992 you were a judge of the district military court in Doboj which was based elsewhere. Did you leave that area, and when, to come to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: As I have already said in the introduction, as of February 1993 I became a judge of the district military court of Doboj which was based in Tesanj, but I stayed in that position only until June of 1993, when due to the conflict between the BH army and the HVO in this territory of Zepca municipality, I was unable to return from Zenica to Tesanj. So I stayed in Zenica and was employed in the district military court in Zenica as of the 25th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you remain a judge in the district military court in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: I remained in that position until it was abolished, and that was in July 1996, when all the judges of the district military court of Zenica were transferred to work in the then-higher court of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what were your duties as a judge of the district military court in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: As a judge of the district military court of Zenica, I acted exclusively as an investigating judge, and from time to time I was also the duty judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when you became a judge of that court or perhaps later, was at some point in time the court subordinated to the 3rd Corps or the BH army?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: No. The district military court of Zenica thought its existence was never subordinated to any military institution, and therefore not to the 3rd Corps command either.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me to whom was that court subordinated in the administrative sense and what was it linked to in the professional jurisdiction system? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: Talking about the administrative links between the Zenica court, in the first period until July 1994 the district military courts were within the jurisdiction of the republican defence ministry, and from then on until they were abolished, district military courts were within the administrative jurisdiction of the republican ministry for justice and administration. With regard to the professional links, it was our duty to abide by the decisions of the then-republican Supreme Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Which was the second instance decision-maker regarding your own judgements?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: Appeals against judgements of district military courts were tried by the Supreme Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but because of the blockade around Sarajevo it had departments in Tuzla and Zenica, first in Tuzla and later in Zenica as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us who the military courts tried, or rather who were they responsible for?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: The exclusive responsibility of district military courts for their duration was to try military personnel, and in some cases, district military courts could also try civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us when military courts could try civilians. Was this stipulated by law or did it depend on practice?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: This was not something that depended on the practice of the courts. The decree forming district military courts stipulated jurisdiction in specific cases for civilians. There were only two possibilities, and those were if there is proof that a civilian had committed a crime against the constitutional order of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina or if the civilian committed a crime against the armed forces, or that is the Army of is the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, which were the offences covered by district military courts?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: District military courts has responsibility to try all criminal offences committed by members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is military personnel; as for civilians, as I have already said, only in cases of two offences against the constitutional order and against the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Judge Ahmetovic, in addition to district military courts in the BH judicial system were there any other courts?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to district military courts in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in those days, there were also regular courts, municipal courts, which were competent for criminal offences committed within the territory of only one municipality; and then there were also higher courts formed at the time for a larger territorial unit and there was the Supreme Court of the Republic Bosnia-Herzegovina as the supreme judicial body.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who did regular courts try?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: They mostly tried civilians, though in some cases they could also try military personnel for criminal offences only if a civilian and a military person jointly perpetrated a criminal offence which did not come within the jurisdiction of district military courts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Judge Ahmetovic, in the legal system of the Republic Bosnia and Herzegovina in addition to courts who -- which are independent in the jurisdiction system, were there any other bodies that were responsible for lawful activities?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were magistrate courts. These are offences that are not criminal offences. If a person commits a minor infringement of the law or of discipline, for example, disturbance of the public law and order, such cases would be tried by magistrate courts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Judge Ahmetovic, do you know whether in addition to independent courts such as regular and district military courts, were there any jurisdiction bodies within the armed forces; and if so, tell us what they were?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to district military courts which had responsibility over military personnel within the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina I remember that a decree was passed envisaging the formation of special military courts in military units which could put on trial only members of the BH army or military personnel which while serving in the BH army committed a crime which could undermine the stability of that military unit which could jeopardise the stability of the front lines. Or if such an act could cause a breakthrough of front lines or fall of front lines, then these special -- then these units had the right to form such special military courts which would -- could on the spot try some persons. And such military courts were not formed, as far as I know, except for one case that I'm aware of of such special military court made by the decision of the commander of the 126th Mountain Brigade, Ilijas, which was in the responsibility of the 1st Corps. But because of the territorial dispersion, the district military courts in Zenica covered that brigade as well. And I am aware that such a court was formed by the brigade commander. But in the course of the proceedings before that court they found that the offence was not so grave and he was forwarded to the district military courts in Zenica to be tried there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Judge Ahmetovic, how did criminal proceedings before a district military court begin? As you have testified, you were investigating judge of that court. Tell me, when and how criminal proceedings began in a district -- in the district military court.

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: In accordance with the valid provisions of the code on criminal procedure taken over from the SFRY and according to which judges of the district military courts, including the Zenica court and myself as judge of that court, would start with an investigation carried out by the investigating judge, that would mark the beginning; which meant that the investigating judge, in accordance with the law on criminal procedure, had the duty to call the suspect, to question that suspect regarding the circumstances of the criminal offence he's being charged with. And if on the basis of his statement and evidence provided by the competent prosecutor that there is grounds to believe that that person committed the crime he is charged with, then an investigation will be started. And this marks the beginning of criminal proceedings against a particular individual.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Judge Ahmetovic, as an investigating judge were you able to decide independently on carrying out investigation because you learned that somebody had committed a crime? And upon whose request could criminal proceedings be instituted?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: The investigating judge, according to the provisions of the code and criminal procedure, had no authority to institute any criminal proceedings himself against anyone until the competent district military prosecutor's office does not [as interpreted] submit a request for starting an investigation against a particular person with a specific factual description of the offence he is charged with and including a legal qualification for that offence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, before criminal proceedings are instituted, that is before the prosecutor submits a request for investigation, which was the body that was in charge of what was known as the pre-criminal proceedings phase or pre-trial phase?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: The only body who was in charge of this pre-trial phase was the district military prosecutor's office or the competent prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You just said that you issued decisions on starting an investigation on the basis of the request of the district military prosecutor. What were the obligations of the investigating judge when receiving such a request?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: According to the provisions of the law on criminal procedure, the investigating judge was duty-bound upon receiving for [as interpreted] the competent military prosecutor's office a request for an investigation to examine the same regarding the factual description and the legal qualification of the criminal offence. And if from the factual description of the offence he would find that it was not properly qualified or that there was no criminal offence and there was no criminal responsibility of that person, he could express his disagreement with the request for an investigation and then ask the criminal Chamber of the same court from which the request for an investigation had been received. So the final decision regarding the factual description and the legal qualification would lie with the court.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Judge Ahmetovic, in the course of the investigation itself, what does the investigating judge actually do? What steps does he take in accordance with the law? What is he entitled to do?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: If the investigating judge is in agreement with the request for an investigation that he received from the prosecutor, the first step that he has to take according to the law is to call up the suspect to question him about the circumstances of the commission of the offence he is charged with. Of course it is implied that that person must be available to the court. And I must say on the basis of practice and my personal experience as an investigating judge, very frequently in the course of criminal proceedings I was not able to reach suspects and very often not even witnesses who were either in territory under control of members of the HVO or the Army of Republika Srpska or such persons had emigrated to third countries and it was simply impossible to reach them. So there were such situations, too. However, in situations when I was able to get hold of the suspect, the first step I would take would be to question that person regarding the circumstances of the commission of the act. Then a decision on an investigation is passed, which is a document allowing the investigating judge to continue with his investigations as envisaged by the competent prosecutor's office or proposed by the prosecutor. Of course, the investigating judge was not bound only by that request. If the investigating judge should find it necessary in the interest of justice and the full establishment of the truth, he could carry out other investigations which he may deem to be necessary at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Judge Ahmetovic, could you now tell me whether the military organ or the military police of that military organ, regardless of whether it was a brigade or a corps, could it order the investigative judge to take certain actions and could the investigative judge be ordered how to take such actions?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not. The investigative judge only had to bear in mind the request for carrying out investigation from the military prosecutor's office; no one else could influence the investigative judge as far as carrying out investigations are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Judge Ahmetovic, tell me, did the investigative judge cooperate with the military police of the army when performing his duties, and if so how would you assess that cooperation, or rather how did the military unit and the military police carry out orders issued by the court?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the investigative judge did cooperate with members of the military police battalion, especially in my case. I cooperated with members of the military police battalion from the 3rd Corps. And in particular, in a situation when we went to on-site investigations together. And later on in the course of the investigation the military police battalion provided all possible support to me as an investigative judge and to the entire district military court in Zenica. They carried out all sorts of orders and provided all forms of support in order to enable the district military court in Zenica to function properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Judge Ahmetovic, could you tell me what -- could you mention some orders that you forwarded to the military police, orders that they carried out, that they had the duty to carry out?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of the investigation, these were my orders: to bring in certain individuals, either suspects or witness who did not want to respond to a call from the court. So the cooperation took the form of bringing in these individuals to the district military court in Zenica. In addition, they carried out all other orders that concerned carrying out certain investigations that were urgent. For example, when an on-site investigation is being carried out, then the court has to use experts from the military police battalion in order to take certain steps. For example, in order to gather evidence at the site, in order to secure the site, in order to secure the evidence at the site, take charge of the evidence, place the evidence in safes where they are kept until the proceedings are instituted. So these are the actions that were taken and the military police battalion provided much assistance to the Zenica district court.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Judge Ahmetovic, on a number of occasions you mentioned on-site investigations. Tell me, according to the law on criminal procedure could the judge sometimes participate in pre-criminal proceedings or pre-trial proceedings before there was a request for proceedings submitted by the prosecutor? And if such, could you mention the situations that this concerned -- if so, could you mention when this took place.

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning I already said that in addition to being an investigative judge I was quite frequently, according to the schedule of the presiding judge, a duty judge. This was a judge who had to carry out on-site investigations if it was necessary when on duty. Duty would last for seven days in a month. The investigative judge would do what was necessary to be done on the basis of law on criminal procedure. And I adhered to these laws when I went to on-site investigations, necessary to state what the judge did at on-site investigations. It would be senseless to mention particular cases. You have cases of murders, traffic accidents, et cetera. I would have to go into all these cases. But the we all though what duty judge or an investigative judge does at an on-site investigation. The duty judge must go to the site whether -- where an incident broke out or to the site where people state that an incident broke out. And he must record the situation there. If there are any changes at the site from the time when the incident occurred up until the time when the duty judge arrives there to carry out the on-site investigation, I believed that it was useless to carry out an investigation at such a site because the site had been tampered with, evidence had been tampered with, perhaps the body, et cetera. And these are the subjects of interest for an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Judge, when you go to an on-site investigation, can you tell me which organ is in charge of an on-site investigation; who issues orders; what kind of orders are issued; and to what extent are certain investigative steps taken in the course of the on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: According to the law of criminal procedure, this is very clear, too. The duty judge is in charge of the on-site investigation and all those present must obey the orders of the duty judge. Naturally, in addition to the duty judge the competent duty prosecutor must be present and other experts who might assist the duty judge when carrying out certain investigations which have to be carried out at the site itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Once the judge is at the site, is at the scene, what is the role of the military police or of the civilian police? Can they continue to do what they think they should do independently or do they have to further abide by orders of the investigative judge?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that the person in charge of the on-site investigation is the duty judge, and no one present is allowed to take any steps unless the duty judge issues an order. The duty judge is the main person in charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Judge, tell me, who is provided with the material, the evidence gathered -- material on the evidence gathered? Once the on-site investigation has been completed, who is provided with this material?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: After the on-site investigation team with the duty judge at its head completes the on-site investigation, the duty judge must compile a written record on the on-site investigation, a record in which he will state what was found in the course of the on-site investigation. And naturally, it's also his duty to refer to all the orders he issued in the course of the on-site investigation. This is also his duty to wait to receive information from the military or civilian police on orders carried out in the course of the on-site investigation. And after all this material evidence has been gathered, together with the record of the on-site investigation, he -- well, he provides all this material to the competent military prosecutor's office, which will then assess all the material provided.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After the judge provides all the material from the on-site investigation together with his record to the competent prosecutor, who becomes the dominus litis, the main person? Who is then in charge of the material and who is in charge of criminal proceedings that might be instituted?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: Since we're speaking about the role of the main person, while continuing to use that term, it's the competent prosecutor who becomes the person who is in charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmetovic, can the military organ or the military police prevent the prosecutor from initiating criminal proceedings or can they in some other way influence the decision taken by the prosecutor as to whether to institute criminal proceedings or not?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: No. No one can influence the competent prosecutor. No one can influence his decision to prosecute an individual or not to prosecute an individual. It's for the prosecutor to decide whether he intends to prosecute someone. No one has any influence on him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you say no one can influence him, can you as a judge influence the prosecutor's decision?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As the investigative judge, having gathered all the evidence, having dealt with all the evidence suggested by the prosecutor or perhaps by the accused or his defence, and having carried out all the actions you believed you should carry out in the interest of justice, what then happens? What is then done up to this stage?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: After I as the investigative judge have carried out all the necessary actions and carried out the request for an investigation and having carried out all the other necessary actions in order to determine what the situation was, when I believe that the investigation is complete I send the record and all the evidence to the competent military prosecutor's office for further assessment. After they have received my case file, the military prosecutor's office in accordance with the law on criminal procedure has a number of possibilities. But it's for the competent prosecutor to decide what to do. No one can influence his decision. And this is quite clearly stated in the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If the prosecutor believes that the evidence gathered is sufficient and that it confirms his belief that a certain individual perpetrated the crime in question, what decision does he take, what sort of document does he draft, and which organ, which body, discusses this decision?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: If the competent prosecutor after having assessed, after having reviewed the entire case file finds that there is sufficient evidence that indicates that someone committed a crime, the prosecutor then brings an indictment to prosecute a certain individual. And this indictment together with the entire file is forwarded to the competent court. In my case it's the military -- district military court. After they receive this indictment, the judge who's in charge of the case will review the indictment and then provide it immediately to the accused and his defence to give them the possibility of objecting to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If the objection is not accepted, what then happens?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: In such a situation the indictment in accordance with the law on criminal procedure comes into legal force and the competent judge seized of the case schedules a trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Judge Ahmetovic, could you now have a look at a document under section 3, documents 1 to 7. And I will now list them. 1 is document 1311; document 2 is document DH155, document number 8; under 3 we have document 1450; number 4, document 1975; number 5, document 1576; number 6, document in -- it says DH306; number 7, document 1977. Once you have had a look at these documents I would like to ask you whether these documents are Prosecution documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we just wish to note for the record that a few of these seven documents just referred to are not translated to English for the time being. It's just for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I didn't quite understand this question because I don't see which documents you're referring to because there are three number 3s.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Number 3 with the heading "Indictment." So there is a set of documents there. It says "Indictment." And then within that group there are seven documents whose numbers I have listed.

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May I help you. You can see the III and a piece of paper that is larger than the rest and the heading on it is "Indictment."

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: I have number 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After the big -- this document you have number 1. And then under number 1 you have a document with the number 1311.

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've found that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So these seven documents, 1 through 7, will you please look at them and tell me whether you recognise in these documents a document of a particular body; and if so, will you tell us what kind of documents and which body is involved.

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: All the documents I have reviewed are very well-known to me. These are indictments of the district military court of the Zenica which was submitted to my district military court in Zenica for further processing. And due to legal considerations, I did not participate in the trials of these persons but I am familiar with these indictments from other trials, such as certain objections to indictments. But I did not take part in trying these persons because that is prohibited. An investigation who is charge -- an investigating judge in charge of an investigation cannot be a trial judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, look first at the first document with the number 1311. This document contains a description of the act that the person is charged with. And after a description of that act, there is a legal qualification of that act. My question to you, Judge, is: Which was the body to be -- the first to suggest a qualification of an offence and which was the body that had the final say regarding the legal qualification of an act?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: According to an unwritten rule from my own experience, criminal reports for criminal offences against individuals were usually filed either by members of the civilian or the military police who would collect evidence about the offence committed and the moment they come to the conclusion that a person has committed or perpetrated, a criminal offence, they file a criminal report in which they describe in which a certain person committed a certain offence and they give a legal qualification of that criminal offence. Of course, that legal qualification was not binding for the prosecutor or for the investigating judge or for the Trial Chamber during the main trial. The only person to finally decide what criminal offence was committed was the competent Trial Chamber of the court.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at the legal qualification in this indictment, you will see that the event in which a person, to appropriate something belonging to Stipe Akrepovic, who was a Croat, pointed an automatic rifle at him, searched his house, and tried to take some property out of that house. This event he qualified as an aggravated burglary according to Article 151 of the Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina. My question to you is: Could the court on the basis of this description change the qualification and qualify it as a different criminal offence if he felt that it could be given a different qualification?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: I have already said that the Trial Chamber or an individual judge who tried the case was not bound by the legal qualification in the indictment, and therefore not by this indictment, either issued against this person for aggravated robbery. The court would decide on the basis of all the evidence produced during the trial. So whatever the individual judge or a Trial Chamber established at trial would be decisive for the qualification of the criminal offence and he would find the suspect guilty or not guilty of that offence, depending on the outcome of the trial. But he was not bound by the legal qualification given here. And if you're asking me for this particular case whether the qualification could be changed, it could if the court found that it was a different offence that was committed. But if the court found that the act corresponded to the one found by the prosecutor, then he would stick with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please look at this indictment number 2, DH155/8. And if you can see from the description, the accused entered the house of the victims Pravdic, Kata, and Stipo - I assume they were also Croats - and according to this description he killed these persons. And the prosecutor suggests that this is the crime of murder under Article 36, paragraph 2. And if the court establishes that this crime was committed, could the trial judge decide to give the crime a different qualification?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: My answer is identical to the previous answer. Every indictment is a separate act and of course it is possible to change the legal qualifications should the court find that the evidence warranted a change in the qualifications. So my answer is the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please look at number 4, document 1975. Here there is stealing of property from abandoned houses and it has been qualified as aggravated theft. Would your answer be identical in a situation when the judge sees this description? Was he the one who decided what qualification he would give to the offence or was it someone else?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: Again, my answer is identical to the previous two. The only person who would have the final say regarding the legal qualification would be either an individual judge or a Trial Chamber, which means the court or the judge. They had the final say.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I see the time. I think it's time for the break. Could the witness be allowed to keep this binder of documents to look through them so that we can save some time later on? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Judge, you will have a rest but during the break you will have an opportunity to look through the documents at the same time. It is half past 10.00 and we will resume at about 5 to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. I give the floor again to Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Judge Ahmetovic, will you please look at the judgements under chapter 4. In this group of documents please look at documents under number 1, which is a judgement of the high court in Zenica, K12/93, dated the 14th of May, 1993; document number 2, which says DH155; which -- document number 7; then document number 3 which says "District military court in Zenica," K212, dated the 4th of August, 1993; document number 4 which says at the top "1367"; then document number 5, DH155; document number 9; the document number 6 which says at the top DH155/12; the document number 8, entitled "High court in Zenica case 67/93," dated the 27th of January, 1994; document number 9; a document number 13 -- 155/13; document number 10 with the document DH155/14. If you had occasion to look through the remaining documents, my question would be first: In these documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The Prosecution doesn't wish to interrupt but wishes to note that the documents 1, 3, 4, and 8 are provided only in the B/C/S version today and documents 1 and 8 are new documents. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as possible, can the Defence draw the attention of the witness to a particular part of the judgement in view of the fact that they are in B/C/S so that the Prosecution can know what is the object of the question and so that we as Judges can appreciate the relevance of the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have told you that, Mr. President. And before we started examining the previous witness, I think we had a discussion on this matter. If a document is in B/C/S only, I shall draw the attention to the witness to the part of the document I wish him to comment on. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since the witness has looked at these documents which were given to the Prosecution a few days ago, could he tell me whether he recognises some court documents and if so, which does he recognise.

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: During the break I reviewed the documents given to me by colleague Residovic. I do recognise these documents of course. These are judgements following trials. I must note that these are judgements of several courts for a period from 1993 to 2000. These are judgements of the high court in Zenica, the district military court in Zenica, the district military court in Travnik, and even the cantonal Zenica court which is the currently active court. The higher court in Zenica no longer exists nor do these district military courts exist. In view of the judgements of the high court of Zenica and even judgements of the district military court in Zenica is something [as interpreted] I would not like to comment on except for these two judgements. I can tell you why I'm familiar with them. One is the judgement of the cantonal court in which I took part together with colleague Veseljak as a trial judge, and this is a judgement dated from 2000, number K67/00, 12th of March, 2000. So I'm very familiar with this judgement and this event because I participated in the trial. I'm also very familiar with the judgement of the district military court of Zenica IK606/94, dated the 21st of December, 1994. I do know Ajanovic, Fahrudin, the suspect, because I carried out the investigation for this criminal case. And I'm also familiar with the judgement of the higher court in Zenica, K194/96, dated the 20th of March, 1997, against the accused Rasid Dzafic. This is a case I investigated while the direct military court in Zenica was still operational. However, after the first-instance judgement of the district military court in Zenica the same judgement was rescinded by the Supreme Court of the republic. And after the district military court was abolished, this case was judged by the Supreme Court. That is why I am familiar with these three judgements.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My questions will not relate to persons and events. I will just ask you to answer some questions you have already testified about and perhaps the documents you have in front of you could serve as illustrations. So the first judgement, which is in B/C/S only and it is a judgement number K12/93 of the higher court in Zenica with respect to the Hazim Maglic, the third accused. Would you look at the explanation on page 10 in the middle of paragraph 3 in which the court judged the circumstances of this event and it is stated in the middle. And with respect to the accused Maglic, Hazim, the court found as mitigating that he was a member of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina before he committed the criminal offence, that he was wounded as such, and that a part of his left lower leg was amputated. I'm asking you, in view of the fact that this case was tried by a regular court though he was a member of the army, is this an example of what you referred to, saying that regular courts were responsible for members of the army if he was a co-perpetrator with a civilian of a particular offence?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the kind of situation I referred to. Mr. Maglic, at the time he committed the offence, was a member of the BH army but he was tried by a regular higher court in Zenica in view of the fact that one or two of the other accused were civilians. And according to the provisions of the law we mentioned, the jurisdiction belongs to the civilian court. I don't know whether I need to comment on all that is stated here. These are just the mitigating facts. The fact that he was a member of the BH army and that he was seriously wounded as a result of which his leg was amputated; this was evaluated as a mitigating offence and requires no further comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In all these judgements contained in this part of the materials there are certain descriptions of the events and there is a legal qualification. My question for you, Judge, is whether this is how the court decided on the facts in question. How were these facts legally qualified? And this is something that confirms your testimony so far. Was it the court that determined a correct qualification of the act in question?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: Since I'm familiar with most of these judgements, I could say that this is a good example of how the court worked. They weren't bound by the legal qualification contained in the indictment. They established the facts at the trial. And on the basis of these facts, they provide this factual description and the legal qualification for which someone was proclaimed guilty.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Judge, could you tell me whether the trial seized of the case could amend the factual description of the prosecutor against the accused?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Judge, tell me, since we have now examined a number of legal qualifications of certain events which have been characterised as aggravated robbery, theft, or murder, could you tell me whether crimes such as murder, theft, violence inflicting physical wounds, et cetera, also had the characteristics of war crimes against the civilian population in accordance with the criminal law adopted from SFRY. And if that was the case, can you tell me why judges decided to qualify these acts in the way they were qualified in the documents we have examined.

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly the exact number, that's Article 142 of the criminal law of the former SFRY, according to this article a reference was made to a war crime against the civilian population. Certain criteria had to be met if such a crime was to be established -- for example, murder, theft, torching property, kidnapping, et cetera. I can't remember all the details, but everything that you have just mentioned in question in that part of the criminal law, this is something that has to be determined. One has to determine whether such crime has been committed or not. I really cannot say now how the Prosecutor qualified certain acts, whether he qualified them as the crime of murder, looting, aggravated robbery, or theft. I couldn't say why he did not qualify such acts as war crimes, but -- in fact, I think that the answer is simple because in the course of establishing the facts, in the course of the investigation, the prosecutor determined that a war crime had not been committed. A murder had been committed in the course of war. And when there is an imminent threat of war in the case of murder, aggravated robbery, looting, theft, and in case of war crime, there were certain prescribed sentences or the sentences prescribed were almost identical. The death sentence could be handed down for such crimes. But the answer is that the prosecutor, on the basis of the facts established in the course of the investigation, determined that the crime committed was the crime of murder and not a war crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Earlier on you said that when you received a request to carry out an investigation, you as the investigative judge tried to determine whether what the prosecutor had stated was in fact the case or whether a crime of another kind had been committed and this is what the trial would decide. Do you remember whether you as the investigative judge or perhaps a trial chamber or the Supreme Court, did they ever inform you in some way that the legal assessment shouldn't be provided as an lex specialis but it should be qualified as a war crime? Do you remember any such decision by an investigating judge, the Supreme Court? Did anyone inform you of the fact that the description of a crime concerned -- of the crime in question was wrong, was erroneous in the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of my career and in the district court in Doboj and in Zenica, I really never came across such a situation, the situation that you have mentioned. The Supreme Court or a branch of the Supreme Court of the Republic Bosnia-Herzegovina never suggested in one of its decisions that the crime concerned wasn't the crime of robbery but that it was a crime that was in fact a war crime. I never came across such decisions from the Supreme Court. Nor were there any objections to that effect. You must bear in mind that in the course of a trial the party had the right to complain, the accused had the right to complain, or the suspect had the right to complain, or even the prosecutor. Given such legal remedy, if -- I don't remember the Chamber or the Chamber of the Supreme Court having taken the sort of decision that you have been mentioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since the accused and their defence counsel probably appealed against certain judgements, against the ones, for example, that we have just examined, tell me with regard to the application of law what was the position of the second-instance Supreme Court? If the law had been violated, could that be appealed or did the Supreme Court had to deal with such cases ex officio?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: Although the parties could appeal and indicate such violations, they could do this on the basis of law of Yugoslavia -- rather, of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. But in this case the Supreme Court of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina had to deal with this ex officio. Even though the parties didn't indicate that the law had been violated, they had to examine such cases. The Supreme Court of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina through its decision had to inform the Chamber that heard -- handed down a judgement that they had violated the law in some way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Judge, could the military police have any influence regardless of their rank in such matters?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: No military units, no civilian institutions, no one else in this specific situation influenced or could influence the work of the court, of the prosecutor's office, or the district military court in Zenica, or the district prosecutor's office in Zenica and the Supreme Court of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This couldn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Judge, since you have said that you worked as an investigative judge, could you tell us about the number of cases instituted against members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina during that period.

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: In the district military court in Zenica I arrived there on the 25th of October, 1993; I was then appointed as an investigative judge. I received such files. And if I'm not mistaken, up until November I think that I dealt with over 200 cases. That was up until the end of 1993. And it's fascinating to say that in the course of 1994 I had over 1.300 cases. Most of them, perhaps 95 per cent of those cases, concerned ABiH members.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For what sort of acts were ABiH members prosecuted? And can you tell me whether you knew what the position of the army was with regard to its members respecting the law?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of my testimony I already said that the Zenica district military court could try members of the military for any crimes covered by the criminal law of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time. There were no exceptions in that respect. It's now difficult to say what sort of crimes were concerned, the crimes that were processed by the Zenica district court. But for crimes such as murder, looting, aggravated theft, which are the most serious ones; then there were also traffic accidents in which people were lightly or seriously wounded. But all forms of crimes were covered.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Judge Ahmetovic, could you now have a look at the document under section 5. Section 5, number 4. The number of the document is 1555. This document is only in B/C/S. Could you please read the title of the document? Have you found the document?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the title of the organ that issued the document, the number of the document. And what is the subject of this document?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: The organ that issued this document is the district military court in Zenica. The number of the document is SU; this means court administration, SU. 247/93, dated the 12th of December, 1993. The subject is a brief analysis of the results of the work from the 1st of January up until the 10th of December, 1993. I don't think I remember this document very well, but the purpose of this document was to point out that the situation was really alarming in the district court in Zenica as far as logistical support is concerned and technical equipment and all other equipment necessary for the work -- for work in the district court in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I do apologise but we have just noticed that document 1555 is already in evidence. The Defence number is DH274, so could the Trial Chamber please be provided with this document because we also have an English translation of this document and this will make it easier for us to put questions to the witness. I think my colleagues have this document and the document in question is DH274.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: While my colleague's looking for this document, could you please read out the fourth and fifth paragraph in the document. You can read it out aloud and I only have one question that I'd like to put to you about this paragraph -- about these paragraphs. "In the course of the year." That's how the fourth paragraph starts: "In the course of the year a total of" ... Could you read that out, please.

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: "In the course of the year a total number of criminal cases (indictments) have been received. 432 which concerned 89 individuals. 250 cases have been solved with -- concerning 573 individuals. 182 cases haven't been dealt with; that concerns 296 individuals." Paragraph 5: "In this course 512 requests for investigations were received concerning 1.346 individuals. And during this course, 339 cases were solved with 844 individuals. This includes cases from 1992 which were dealt with in 1993. 172 cases haven't been solved concerning 502 individuals. 13 cases from this period -- 13 cases are from 1992 and that concerned 32 individuals."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Judge Ahmetovic, are these numbers that indicate the volume of work that the district military court had to deal with in 1993, that's the period that this brief analysis is concerned with?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Judge, could you please have a look at document under 3. The number of the document is P771, and could you tell me whether you're familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this document. This was drafted by the president of my cantonal court in Zenica. And I participated in drafting this document. I helped my -- the president of the court with providing this information. I think it was a request -- it concerned a request from the prosecutor from that tribunal. I'm well familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Judge, on the second page of this document in paragraph 4 it says that with regard to ABiH members according to the evidence of the court not a single case has been dealt with during the period concerned, not during the period during which the court was in existence. Since you drafted this document at the request of the prosecutor's office of that tribunal, could you tell us what this concerns. We have just had a look at a document which deals with a number of cases in 1993.

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that the subject of this document is a report on how many were processed for war crimes by the district military court in Zenica. And the comment made by the president of the judge [as interpreted] in paragraph 4 probably has to do with that. According to the court's evidence, no cases have been processed that concern ABiH members during the period concerned and during the existence of the court. This means in front of the district Zenica court not a single ABiH member was prosecuted for a war crime. And that's all that this paragraph has to do with. I don't see what else it could concern.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Colleague Ahmetovic, after the war as an investigating judge or as a judge of the cantonal court, did you in any point in time come across cases linked to events in Dusina that may have been processed and forwarded to the court?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC
utterances.text: After the cantonal court in Zenica was formed in June 1997, I held the position of investigating judge. And for the following two years, I was judge for administrative disputes. And from the end of 1999 and the beginning of 2000, I became an investigating judge again primarily for criminal offences of war crimes. And I'm familiar with the case you're referring to, the case of Dusina through a case that I investigated as an investigating judge. And that case, to the best of my recollection, was forwarded to the cantonal court in Zenica by the cantonal court of Central Bosnia, that is from Travnik. And by their decision they declared themselves incompetent and forwarded the file to Zenica. And a month or two later in accordance with the Roman rule root, the cantonal court received approval from the prosecutor's office that it may process one person which The Hague's prosecutor's office classified as category A. So on the basis of documents provided by Travnik to the prosecutor's office in The Hague, the prosecutor found that only for Edem Hakanovic is there specific evidence that a person had committed a war crime against the civilian population under Article 153 of the Criminal Code of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And approval was given to the cantonal court in Zenica to process the case against this person. I haven't finished yet. After the court received such permission, the prosecutor's office in Zenica filed a request for an investigation against this person, and this request was addressed to me. And I acted in the case in the way I've already described.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me go back a little.
